code_label: Systematic comparison of quantum generative models
text_span: This work systematically compares a broad range of techniques to guide quantum computing practitioners when deciding which models and methods to use in their applications.
rationale: States the paper's main aim and comparative scope.

code_label: Continuous versus discrete circuit architectures
text_span: We compare fundamentally different architectural ansatzes of parametric quantum circuits: 1. A continuous architecture, which produces continuous-valued data samples, and 2. a discrete architecture, which samples on a discrete grid.
rationale: Defines the two main quantum model families under study.

code_label: Min-max and PIT preprocessing compared
text_span: We also compare the performance of different data transformations: the min-max and the probability integral transforms.
rationale: Identifies the preprocessing methods benchmarked in the study.

code_label: QCBM and QGAN training methods
text_span: We use two popular training methods: 1. quantum circuit Born machines (QCBM), and 2. quantum generative adversarial networks (QGAN).
rationale: Specifies the two quantum training paradigms evaluated.

code_label: Quantum models need similar or fewer parameters
text_span: For all data sets, our quantum models require similar or fewer parameters than their classical counterparts.
rationale: One of the paper's headline findings on parameter efficiency.

code_label: Two orders of magnitude parameter reduction
text_span: In the extreme case, the quantum models require two orders of magnitude less parameters.
rationale: Highlights the strongest reported parameter-efficiency result.

code_label: Discrete copula architecture outperforms others
text_span: we empirically find that a variant of the discrete architecture, which learns the copula of the probability distribution, outperforms all other methods.
rationale: States the paper's most important empirical performance conclusion.

code_label: Industrial motivation for quantum generative modeling
text_span: As an industry consortium, QUTAC1, encompassing twelve of the largest German companies, we are interested in understanding the value that quantum technologies can bring, in the short and long term, to our respective industries.
rationale: Explains the industrial motivation behind the study.

code_label: Classical GAN limitations motivate quantum exploration
text_span: These challenges present an opportunity for quantum computing [3].
rationale: Links classical generative-model limitations to the quantum research opportunity.

code_label: Quantum systems as probabilistic generators
text_span: Since quantum systems are inherently probabilistic, quantum states are a natural choice to model probability distributions.
rationale: Provides the conceptual basis for using quantum states in generative modeling.

code_label: Discrete models learn copulas
text_span: the discrete architectures are additionally divided into copula and standard variants.
rationale: Introduces the discrete copula variant as a distinct architecture.

code_label: PIT naturally matched to copula architecture
text_span: the probability integral transform of the data, which is naturally matched to the discrete copula architecture but can also be used with others.
rationale: Explains why PIT is especially relevant for the copula model.

code_label: KL divergence used as performance metric
text_span: As it is common practice in the field, we report the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the probability density of the training data and that of the generated samples as our performance measure.
rationale: Identifies the main evaluation metric used throughout the paper.

code_label: Large simulation study with open-sourced code
text_span: In a total, we ran of over 1200 numerical experiments and comparisons.
rationale: Indicates the scale of the benchmarking effort.

code_label: Discrete models faster but use more qubits
text_span: The discrete models use more qubits and are faster to train and sample, whereas the continuous models are smaller, but training and sampling will take substantially longer on quantum hardware.
rationale: Summarizes a key resource trade-off between architectures.

code_label: Copula plus PIT has an edge
text_span: we show that the copula architecture, paired with the probability integral transform, has an edge in terms of training performance regarding the other quantum architectures tested in this work.
rationale: States the paper's preferred configuration based on training performance.

code_label: Generative modeling learns an unknown distribution
text_span: a generative model attempts to learn an unknown probability distribution Q by modeling an approximated probability distribution P(θ) which is parameterized by a set of variables θ.
rationale: Defines the general generative-modeling setup used in the paper.

code_label: GAN adversarial training structure
text_span: the generator attempts to fool the discriminator by generating data which is indistinguishable from the real training data and the discriminator learns to distinguish data created by the generator from the training data.
rationale: Describes the classical GAN mechanism used as a baseline.

code_label: QCBM learns a unitary mapping to a target state
text_span: The task is to learn a unitary operator U(θ) that maps an initial state, usually |0⟩n = |0⟩⊗n, prepared in an n-qubit system, to some target state which encodes the probability distribution we want to learn
rationale: Defines the QCBM learning objective.

code_label: QCBM optimization minimizes KL divergence
text_span: θ∗ = arg min θ CKL(Q, P(θ))
rationale: States the optimization target for QCBM training.

code_label: QGAN uses quantum generator and classical discriminator
text_span: we consider only the case where the generator is quantum, to reduce the number of qubits required.
rationale: Specifies the QGAN design choice used in the experiments.

code_label: Min-max normalization definition
text_span: In min-max normalization each data point is shifted such that it lies between 0 and 1:
rationale: Introduces the first preprocessing transformation.

code_label: PIT produces uniform marginals and copula
text_span: The transformation of the original probability distribution to the distribution of its uniformly distributed cumulative marginals is known as the copula.
rationale: Defines the PIT/copula transformation central to the paper.

code_label: PIT simplifies structure by learning copula
text_span: This transformation has the purpose of simplifying the structure of the data, as now all variables are correlated and uniformly distributed, independently of the nature of the original probability distribution.
rationale: Explains the intended modeling benefit of PIT preprocessing.

code_label: Continuous architecture outputs expectation values
text_span: The output of the model, for one sample, is given by the feature vector
rationale: Introduces the continuous model's output representation.

code_label: Continuous architecture needs external noise
text_span: This architecture requires an external source of entropy to produce samples, analogous to the classical generative models.
rationale: Notes a key design requirement of the continuous ansatz.

code_label: Discrete architecture samples directly from measurement
text_span: This means that the probability amplitudes ci directly encode the values of the learned probability distribution.
rationale: Explains how the discrete model represents the distribution.

code_label: Discrete architecture is measurement efficient
text_span: Therefore, this type of architecture allows for very efficient sampling, only a single shot evaluation is required per sample.
rationale: States the sampling efficiency advantage of the discrete architecture.

code_label: Copula circuit enforces uniform marginals
text_span: This construction ensures that, when sampling from this circuit, the marginal probabilities are uniform and thus enforces the structure of the copula.
rationale: Describes the structural property of the copula circuit.

code_label: Classical and quantum model size compared by parameters
text_span: We vary the number of model parameters θ for each model as we study their scaling behavior.
rationale: Explains the scaling comparison strategy.

code_label: Increasing parameters lowers KL divergence
text_span: A trend seen over all data sets and model varieties was that increasing the number of parameters decreased the KL divergence.
rationale: Reports a broad empirical trend across experiments.

code_label: Example of large quantum parameter savings
text_span: a classical GAN with a min-max normalization with 9475 parameters achieves a minimum KL of 0.089, whereas a QGAN with a discrete copula architecture, PIT normalization, and 54 parameters achieves a KL of 0.029.
rationale: Provides a concrete example of quantum parameter efficiency.

code_label: Quantum models outperform classical on X and O
text_span: We see that for the O and X data sets for both 2D and 3D, all quantum models performed better than the classical models with similar numbers of parameters.
rationale: Summarizes a major comparative result.

code_label: Discrete copula consistently outperforms classical
text_span: the discrete copula models consistently outperforming the classical ones.
rationale: Highlights the strongest recurring performance pattern.

code_label: QCBM training uses CMA-ES
text_span: For all architectures, we minimized Eq. (6) via a state-of-the-art gradient-free method, CMA-ES [58].
rationale: Specifies the optimizer used for QCBM training.

code_label: QGAN training uses gradient descent
text_span: All QGANs were trained by gradient descent methods.
rationale: Specifies the optimizer family used for QGAN training.

code_label: QGAN slightly better than QCBM
text_span: Overall, QGAN performs slightly better than the QCBM for both 2D and 3D data, although the differences are smaller than the variations due to circuit architecture and normalization.
rationale: States the relative performance of the two quantum training methods.

code_label: Discrete copula with PIT most performant in 2D
text_span: In the 2D case, the discrete copula architecture with a PIT normalization was the most performant, and the standard discrete architecture and both continuous models were worse.
rationale: Identifies the best-performing 2D configuration.

code_label: PIT helps discrete architectures more than continuous
text_span: For the 2D and 3D data sets, the PIT normalization outperformed the min-max normalization for the discrete architecture.
rationale: Reports a preprocessing effect specific to discrete models.

code_label: Continuous architecture shows no clear PIT advantage
text_span: Here, there is no clear advantage regarding the data transformations.
rationale: Summarizes the continuous-model training observation.

code_label: Training stability depends on architecture
text_span: the stability of training a QGAN is highly dependent on the model architecture, see Appendix VII D.
rationale: States a caveat about training stability and architecture dependence.

code_label: PIT reduces mode collapse in discrete copula QGANs
text_span: When using PIT data, we observed fewer mode collapses or similar instabilities, that are common to GANs, when compared with min-max normalized data for the discrete copula architecture.
rationale: Reports a stability benefit of PIT for discrete copula QGANs.

code_label: Need to explore higher-dimensional data
text_span: In future work, we will explore the interplay of learning processes and generalization with higher dimensional data.
rationale: Explicit future research direction on scaling to higher dimensions.

code_label: Generalization remains open
text_span: the quality of the generalization, i. e., how well the model can generate data that was not present in the training set.
rationale: Identifies generalization as an open issue beyond the current study.

code_label: Need to test on real hardware and noise
text_span: future research must also explore the effects of decoherence in generative modeling.
rationale: States a future work item related to hardware noise and realism.
